title: Check for Open Recalls Before You Buy Out Your Lease
description: Recall letters often never reach lease drivers. How to run your VIN through NHTSA's free lookup before a buyout, what it misses, and what to do if a recall is open.
body:
Before you buy out a lease, run the car's VIN through the federal recall lookup. It takes about a minute, it is free, and it tells you whether the car you are about to own has a safety repair still waiting. Once you sign, the car is yours, and so is anything left unfixed.

Why lease drivers miss recalls

During a lease, the leasing company owns the car. Recall letters go to whatever name and address the manufacturer has on file, and that may not be yours. Plenty of people drive a leased car for three years without ever seeing a recall notice, even when one applies. The buyout is the moment to catch up.

How to check

  • Find the VIN. NHTSA says the 17-character vehicle identification number is on the lower left of the windshield. It is also on your registration card and may be on your insurance card. Your lease paperwork and payoff letter list it too.
  • Enter it at NHTSA.gov/Recalls. The result shows any open safety recall for that specific car. A clean result reads "0 unrepaired recalls associated with this VIN."
  • Look for a red box. NHTSA flags open "do not drive" and fire-risk recalls in a red box at the top of the results. If you see one, take it seriously before you drive the car anywhere, including to sign the paperwork.

What the lookup does not show

NHTSA is clear that the search has limits. It does not list recalls that have already been repaired. It may not show some very recent recalls whose affected VINs have not been identified yet. It does not cover safety recalls more than 15 years old, unless the manufacturer provides more coverage. A clean result today is a good sign, not a guarantee, so it is worth checking again a few weeks after you buy.

If a recall is open

NHTSA says recall repairs are free at an authorized dealership. The manufacturer has to fix the problem by repairing or replacing the part, offering a refund, or in rare cases buying the car back. That obligation follows the car, so it does not matter whether the leasing company or you holds the title when the work is done.

  • Book the repair now. Call a franchised dealer for that brand with the VIN and the recall number. You can usually get it done before the buyout closes or right after.
  • Do not expect a lower payoff. Your purchase price is the residual set in your contract. An open recall is a repair you are owed, not usually a discount. Ask your leasing company in writing if you want to raise it.
  • Ask about parts. Sometimes a recall is announced before the fix is ready. Ask the dealer when parts are expected and what they advise in the meantime.
  • Keep the paperwork. Ask for the repair order showing the recall was completed. It helps if you sell the car later.

Stay on the list after you buy

Once the car is in your name, update your address with the manufacturer so future notices reach you. NHTSA's free SaferCar app can also alert you when a new safety recall is issued for a vehicle you have added.

Common questions

Does an open recall stop me from buying out my lease?

Not by itself. The buyout is a purchase under your lease contract. The recall repair is a separate, free fix from the manufacturer, and it is smart to get it done around the time you buy.

Who pays for a recall repair on a car I just bought out?

NHTSA says recall repairs are free at an authorized dealership. That applies whoever owns the car.

Is the free recall lookup the same as a vehicle history report?

No. The NHTSA lookup covers open safety recalls only. Accident, title and service history come from other sources, and your own records for the lease are a good place to start.
